screens.title: Putting It All Together
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we will synthesize how a transaction moves through a Hyperledger Fabric network and how the network is assembled so those transactions can run reliably. You will learn the five-phase transaction flow starting from a client application constructing a signed proposal, through endorsement and assembly, to ordering, validation, and final ledger commitment. We will also walk through the high-level setup steps for a multi-organization network: defining topology, generating cryptographic identities, producing configuration artifacts, deploying components, creating channels, and activating chaincode. A concrete example you will keep in mind is a two-organization test network where a client asks both organizations to endorse an asset transfer; we will use that to explain endorsement policies and version concurrency checks. As you follow the sequence, pay attention to common points of failure: missing certificates, mis-set environment variables, or incorrect endorsement policy definitions can stop a transaction or a channel from forming. By the end of this chapter you should be able to trace where to look when a transaction is rejected and what artifacts are required to bring up a minimal Fabric network. Reflect on which step — identity, endorsement, ordering, or validation — most affects security in your environment.

keyIdea.title: Why this chapter matters
keyIdea.text: Understanding the end-to-end transaction flow and the network setup steps lets you debug failures, design secure endorsement policies, and deploy resilient Fabric networks.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.6 › Putting It All Together
Putting It All Together
Trace a complete transaction and learn the network setup steps that let transactions execute securely.

This chapter connects the runtime transaction lifecycle — proposal, endorsement, ordering, validation, commitment — with the static artifacts you must create when provisioning a Fabric network. Follow a two-organization example to see how identity, endorsement policies, ordering, and configuration artifacts interact.

Keep an eye on identity files and environment configuration: those are frequent sources of failure during setup and testing.

In this lesson
A paced walkthrough of transaction phases and the step-by-step network setup commands you will use for a minimal two-org network.
Explore Key Topics
Transaction Flow
Five phases from proposal to commitment that guarantee consistency.
Network Setup
Topology, crypto generation, and configuration artifacts you must produce.
Troubleshooting
Common mistakes and debugging pointers for identity and config issues.
Client
Constructs signed proposal
Endorsing Peers
Execute chaincode, produce read/write sets and endorsements
Ordering Service
Sequences transactions into blocks and broadcasts
Key Idea

Security and consistency are enforced by separating execute (endorsement) from order (consensus) and final validate/commit steps at peers.

Coming up
We will animate the five-step transaction flow, then shift into a terminal-style walkthrough of the cryptogen and configtxgen commands used to provision a minimal two-organization network.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to trace a full transaction lifecycle and identify where each component participates. First, you will map the journey from a client-constructed, signed transaction proposal through endorsement, assembly, ordering, and final validation and commitment on the ledger. Second, you will explain how endorsing peers produce read/write sets and signed proposal responses and why peers do not update their ledger during endorsement. Third, you will outline the high-level steps required to create a multi-organization Fabric network: define topology, generate cryptographic material, produce configuration artifacts with configtxgen, deploy components, create channels, and deploy chaincode. Finally, you will recognize common points of failure—incorrect file paths, misconfigured environment variables, or broken endorsement policies—and apply basic debugging steps. These objectives guide what to practice: tracing a transaction, inspecting proposal responses, and running the cryptogen and configtxgen commands conceptually. Each skill matters because they let you design secure policies, locate failures fast, and set up a network that processes transactions predictably.

screens.title: How you'll use these skills
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives translate into practical abilities. You will be able to inspect a proposal response to verify endorsements and read/write sets, and then use that information to assemble and submit a transaction to the ordering service. You will understand why the ordering service only sequences transactions and does not execute chaincode, which helps you reason about where performance bottlenecks occur. On the setup side, you will conceptually run cryptogen to create MSP directories and then use configtxgen to generate a genesis block and channel transactions that embed those MSPs. A common example is generating crypto material for two organizations, then producing a channel transaction that lists them both so they can participate. Finally, you will practice troubleshooting steps: checking file paths, verifying that the MSP directories exist, confirming that environment variables like the Fabric config path are set correctly, and examining endorsement policy definitions in the channel config. These practical checks help you move from understanding to applying and maintaining a Fabric network.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.6 › How you'll use these skills
Practical outcomes
Inspecting proposals
Learn to read a proposal response to confirm which keys were read and what writes a transaction would apply. This helps explain why a later VCC failure occurred.
Ordering vs Execution
Understand that ordering purely sequences transactions. Execution and endorsement happen at peers and determine validity before state is updated.
Artifact generation flow
Combine cryptogen or Fabric CA outputs with configtxgen artifacts so your genesis and channel config reference correct MSPs.
Debug checklist
Verify file paths, MSP presence, environment variables, and endorsement policy definitions first when things fail.

screens.title: Five Phases of a Transaction
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through the canonical five-phase transaction flow as a single, connected process. First, a client application constructs a transaction proposal. This proposal names a chaincode function, passes arguments, specifies a channel, and is signed with the client's X.509 identity. For example, a Node. js client might prepare a transfer from account A to account B and sign the proposal with its certificate. Second, the proposal goes to endorsing peers. Each endorsing peer verifies the client's signature, executes the chaincode against its local state database, and produces a read/write set and a signed proposal response. Remember: peers do not write state at this phase. Third, the client collects endorsements as required by the endorsement policy, assembles them with the original proposal and its signature, and submits the assembled transaction to the ordering service. An everyday misconception is to expect the ordering service to validate endorsements; it does not. Fourth, the ordering service sequences transactions into blocks, signs them, and broadcasts blocks to committing peers. Fifth, each committing peer validates endorsements against policy and performs a version concurrency control check to ensure read-set versions are still current. If both checks pass, the write set is applied and the block appended; if not, the transaction is recorded as invalid but stays on the chain. Think of execution and endorsement as a hypothesis check and ordering as the shared timeline that gives all peers the same view of history.

keyIdea.title: Core Sequence
keyIdea.text: Execution/endorsement is separate from ordering and commit; this separation preserves determinism and security.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.6 › Five Phases of a Transaction
Transaction Phases
A deterministic sequence that enforces approvals and concurrency rules.
1. Transaction Proposal
Client prepares signed proposal with chaincode, args, and channel ID.
2. Endorsement
Endorsing peers execute chaincode, produce read/write sets, and sign proposal responses.
3. Assembly & Submission
Client gathers endorsements, assembles the transaction, and submits it to ordering.
4. Ordering
Ordering service sequences transactions into blocks and broadcasts to peers.
5. Validation & Commitment
Committing peers validate endorsement policy and perform VCC before applying writes and appending the block.
Key Takeaway

Execution produces a proposal response; ordering arranges time; validation enforces correctness before state changes.

Annotated Flow (scenario)
Scenario: A client requests transfer of 10 tokens from Org1 to Org2. Client signs proposal and sends to peer0.org1 and peer0.org2. Each peer simulates and returns a read/write set. Client collects both endorsements, assembles the transaction, and submits it. Orderer places the transaction in a block and broadcasts. Peers validate that the read versions match current ledger state; if unchanged, peers update state; otherwise transaction is marked invalid.
Common misconception: expecting ordering to check endorsements or execute chaincode. It only sequences and groups transactions.
Check your understanding
  • Which component produces read/write sets?
  • Does endorsement change the ledger state immediately?
  • Who performs the final VCC check?

screens.title: Transaction Proposal and Endorsement
screens.narratorSegment: A transaction proposal is the client's initial request to execute a chaincode function. It contains the chaincode name, the function to invoke, any arguments, the channel identifier, and it is cryptographically signed by the client's identity. For example, a client asking chaincode to create an asset will include the asset fields as arguments and sign the proposal with its X.509 certificate and private key. When an endorsing peer receives the proposal, it verifies the client's signature to authenticate the request and then simulates execution of the chaincode against its local state. The important result here is the read/write set: the peer records which ledger keys were read and which keys would be written. The peer packages the read/write set into a proposal response and signs that response with the peer's private key to create an endorsement. A recurring misconception is to think a peer commits state at endorsement time; it does not. The endorsement is simply a cryptographic attestation that the peer, given its current state, produced that read/write set. Understanding this separation helps you reason about why read versions matter for later VCC checks and why collecting the correct set of endorsements is critical to satisfy policy before submission.

keyIdea.title: Proposal vs Endorsement
keyIdea.text: The proposal describes intent and is signed by the client; endorsements are signed attestations by peers verifying simulated execution and producing read/write sets.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.6 › Proposal & Endorsement
Transaction Proposal
Contents: function, args, channel ID, client signature (X.509).
Client example
Prepare a createAsset invocation with asset ID and owner fields, sign with client certificate before sending to endorsing peers.
Endorsing peer behavior
Verify client signature, execute chaincode simulation, produce read/write set, and sign the proposal response to create an endorsement.
Common-mistake

Expecting a peer to commit state during endorsement. Endorsement only simulates and attests; commit happens after validation.

Read/Write Set Example
Read: asset:ID -> version 5. Write: asset:ID owner -> "Org2". The read version is carried forward so later VCC can detect intervening writes.
Check your understanding
Why must the peer sign the proposal response? What information in a response is vital for later validation?

screens.title: Assembling and Submitting the Transaction
screens.narratorSegment: After you receive proposal responses, the client must collect the endorsements required by the chaincode's endorsement policy and assemble them into a single transaction. Assembly means bundling the original proposal, every collected endorsement, and the client's own signature into a transaction envelope. For example, if the endorsement policy requires signatures from Org1 and Org2, you need at least one signed response from a peer in each organization. Only a fully assembled, signed transaction can be submitted to the ordering service. A common misunderstanding is to assume the client should wait for ordering to validate endorsements; ordering only sequences transactions and does not evaluate endorsement policies. When the assembled transaction is sent to the ordering service, it becomes part of the global input stream the orderer uses to produce blocks. If endorsements are insufficient or missing, committing peers will later mark the transaction invalid during validation. So as a developer or operator, you must ensure the client is programmed to gather the required endorsements and to handle the case where endorsements fail or peers return different read/write sets. The client should also sign the assembled transaction to prove origin during ordering and later validation.

keyIdea.title: Client responsibility
keyIdea.text: The client assembles and signs the full transaction; ordering does not validate endorsements.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.6 › Assembling & Submission
Assemble endorsements
Bundle: proposal + endorsements + client signature.
// Pseudocode representation
proposal = { chaincode: 'asset', fcn: 'transfer', args: ['A','B', '10'], channel: 'mychannel' }
endorsements = [signedResp1, signedResp2]
transaction = { proposal, endorsements, clientSignature }
submitToOrdering(transaction)
Misconception

Ordering does not check endorsements or run chaincode. It only sequences transactions into blocks.

Example: two-org policy
If the policy requires Org1 and Org2, the client must collect at least one endorsement signed by a peer from each organization before submission. If one endorsement is missing, the transaction will fail endorsement policy validation later.
Check your understanding
How should a client behave when peers return different read/write sets? What must the client include to prove transaction origin?

screens.title: Ordering Service Role and Block Formation
screens.narratorSegment: The ordering service's purpose is to create a single deterministic sequence of transactions for all peers. It receives fully assembled transactions from clients across organizations, arranges them chronologically according to its consensus algorithm, groups them into blocks, and then signs and broadcasts those blocks to all committing peers on the channel. For example, transactions from different clients are interleaved into an ordered stream so every peer processes the same sequence when validating and committing. The ordering service does not execute chaincode or validate endorsement policies — its responsibility is sequencing and availability. A practical implication is that ordering performance influences throughput and latency: batch timeouts and batch sizes affect how quickly a transaction appears in a block. A typical misconception is expecting the orderer to resolve endorsement conflicts. It cannot; if two transactions conflict on the same state, the first that commits will make the second fail its VCC check at commit time. Understanding this separation helps operators tune batch parameters and architects decide where to place ordering nodes and how many are needed for fault tolerance. Ordering Service Role and Block Formation means order only sequences and groups transactions into blocks; peers are responsible for validation and state changes.. In practical terms, sequencing, batching, and block distribution. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Order only sequences and groups transactions into blocks; peers are responsible for validation and state changes.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.6 › Ordering Service
Ordering and Blocks
Orderer sequences transactions and forms blocks which it signs and broadcasts to peers.
Batching considerations
BatchTimeout and BatchSize determine when transactions are placed into a block, affecting latency and throughput tradeoffs.
Operator note

Tune ordering parameters to balance block frequency with network and peer processing capacity. Orderer does not validate endorsements.

Example behavior
Multiple clients submit transactions; the orderer deterministically sequences them and creates a signed block which it sends to all channel peers. Peers then validate in that same order.
Misconception check
Do not rely on ordering to enforce endorsement policy or to execute chaincode. Validation occurs at peers during commit.

screens.title: Validation and Commitment at Committing Peers
screens.narratorSegment: When a committing peer receives a block, it processes each transaction in order and performs two key checks before applying any write set. The first is endorsement policy validation: the peer verifies that the collected endorsements satisfy the chaincode's policy, confirming the right organizations signed the proposal response. The second is the version concurrency control check, which ensures that the ledger state read by the endorsing peers has not changed since endorsement. This is implemented by comparing the read set versions recorded at endorsement time with the current versions in the state database. If both checks pass, the peer applies the write set and appends the block; if either fails, the transaction is marked invalid and its write set is not applied. An important consequence is that transactions are still visible on the blockchain when invalid; the record exists but has no effect on state. A common mistake is to confuse an invalid transaction with a missing record. Even failed transactions are recorded, which preserves an auditable trail. This mechanism ensures consistency across peers and prevents stale endorsements from changing up-to-date state.

keyIdea.title: Validation gates
keyIdea.text: Endorsement policy and VCC checks at commit time are the final gates that determine whether a transaction updates ledger state.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.6 › Validation & Commitment
Validation Steps
Each transaction is checked for correct endorsements and unchanged read versions before writes are applied.
1. Endorsement policy validation
Confirm endorsements are from required organizations and peers per the chaincode policy.
2. Version Concurrency Control (VCC)
Compare read-set versions captured during endorsement with current state versions to detect concurrent updates.
Important

Even invalid transactions are recorded on the blockchain to preserve an immutable audit trail; they simply do not change state.

Example: concurrent update
If peer A endorses a transfer using read version v5, but another transaction updates the same key and commits before this block is processed, the VCC check will detect the mismatch and mark the transaction invalid.
Check your understanding
Why is recording invalid transactions important? How does VCC prevent lost updates?

screens.title: Defining Network Topology
screens.narratorSegment: Before you generate crypto or configuration artifacts you must decide on network topology: how many organizations will participate, how many peers each organization runs, and how many orderer nodes are required for the chosen consensus. For a minimal two-organization development network you might select one peer per organization and a single ordering node; for production you would plan multiple peers and a fault-tolerant orderer cluster. These choices affect endorsement policies, availability, and fault tolerance. For example, an endorsement policy requiring endorsements from three organizations implies you must have at least that many participating signing identities. A common mistake is configuring an endorsement policy that references organizations or MSP IDs that are not included in the channel configuration; this prevents transactions from ever meeting policy. Another frequent issue is under-sizing the ordering service which causes high latency under load. The topology decision also informs your cryptographic material generation: each organization needs its own MSP and CA roots embedded in genesis and channel artifacts. Treat topology as an architectural decision that sets constraints for every following setup step. Defining Network Topology means topology decisions determine endorsement capability, fault tolerance, and which msp identities must be included in configuration artifacts.. In practical terms, organizations, peers, and orderer nodes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Topology matters
keyIdea.text: Topology decisions determine endorsement capability, fault tolerance, and which MSP identities must be included in configuration artifacts.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.6 › Defining Topology
Topology Decisions
Choose number of orgs, peers per org, and ordering nodes based on availability and policy needs.
Impact on endorsement
Your endorsement policy must reference MSPs present on the channel. If you require endorsements from an org that isn't on the channel, transactions cannot meet policy.
Orderer sizing
Batch sizes and number of orderer nodes affect throughput and fault tolerance. Consider expected load when planning nodes.
Common-mistake

Defining an endorsement policy that cannot be satisfied by the organizations on a channel.

Example topology (conceptual)
Two organizations, one peer each, and a single orderer for a minimal development setup. For production add peers per org and an etcdraft orderer cluster for resilience.
Check your understanding
If your policy needs two org signatures, what happens when one org is offline? How does topology choice affect availability?

screens.title: Generating Cryptographic Material (cryptogen)
screens.narratorSegment: Generating cryptographic material creates the identities and trust anchors that every component uses. In development you can use the cryptogen utility to produce X.509 certificates and private keys for orderers, peers, and users. For example, a typical command is: cryptogen generate --config=./crypto-config. yaml --output=./organizations. The crypto-config file lists organizations, domains, and node counts. After running cryptogen you should see MSP directories for each org under the output path, containing certificates and keystore material. A helpful self-check is to inspect organizations/peerOrganizations/org1. example. com/msp to confirm the admincerts and cacerts entries exist. Remember that production environments typically use Fabric CA instead of cryptogen to support dynamic enrollment and certificate lifecycle management. A common setup mistake is pointing configtxgen or peer commands at the wrong FABRIC_CFG_PATH; if the environment variable is unset or points to a different folder, commands will fail or produce artifacts referencing incorrect paths. Conceptually, cryptogen results become the identities that configtxgen will embed into genesis and channel artifacts. Generating Cryptographic Material (cryptogen) means cryptogen produces development certificates and msp directories used to identify organizations, peers, orderers, and users.. screens.title: Common Setup Failures and Bottlenecks
screens.narratorSegment: When bringing up a Fabric network or troubleshooting a failed transaction there are recurring root causes to check first. One common class of failures is file and path misconfiguration: cryptographic materials or MSP directories referenced by peers or configtxgen are missing or pointed at the wrong location. Inspecting the expected MSP paths under your organizations output folder often reveals the issue. Another frequent problem is environment variables like FABRIC_CFG_PATH not pointing to the directory containing configtx. yaml and connection profiles; this causes config commands to produce incorrect artifacts. Network connectivity or firewall rules can prevent peers and orderers from communicating, so verify that the advertised hostnames and ports are reachable. Mis-specified endorsement policies in the channel configuration are a logical error: if the policy requires endorsements from organizations not present on the channel, transactions will never meet policy. Performance bottlenecks often stem from small peer resources or orderer batch settings that create latency under load. A simple debugging workflow: confirm MSPs exist, verify environment variables, check logs for signature verification failures, and ensure endorsement policy matches intended organizations. This focused checklist helps you quickly find the likely cause before deeper investigation.

screens.title: Security Considerations and Best Practices
screens.narratorSegment: Security and maintainability are essential for a healthy Fabric network. At a minimum, protect private keys and MSP directories generated by cryptogen or Fabric CA: these artifacts are the root of trust for organizations, peers, and orderers. Use strong, unique passwords for CA servers and limit access to folders containing keystores. Back up critical configuration files and ledger data regularly so you can recover from node failure or data loss. Another practical point is to rotate certificates and plan for revocation in production environments, which is why Fabric CA is recommended for lifecycle management in non-development contexts. When debugging, never expose private keys or paste them into logs; treat keys as highly sensitive secrets. A frequent misconception is believing development shortcuts like sharing admin keys are harmless; they are acceptable only in isolated test networks and become severe risks in production. Finally, create operational runbooks that document the steps to recreate or restore MSP and config artifacts so teams can recover quickly. These maintenance habits reduce downtime and prevent accidental security breaches. screens.title: Key Concepts — Part 1
screens.narratorSegment: Let's consolidate the essential concepts you saw in this chapter. First, the transaction flow is a sequence of phases: proposal, endorsement, assembly, ordering, and validation/commitment. Each phase has a distinct responsibility. Second, a transaction proposal originates from the client and contains the invocation details and client signature; it is not the committed transaction. Third, an endorsement is a peer's cryptographic signature over a proposal response that contains the read/write set resulting from executing chaincode against the peer's local state. These three concepts form the backbone of how Fabric ensures that only properly authorized, non-conflicting transactions change ledger state. Keep these definitions in mind as you trace transactions or generate configuration artifacts, because they point to where you should inspect signatures, versions, and policies when debugging. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we will synthesize how a transaction moves through a Hyperledger Fabric network and how the network is assembled so those transactions can run reliably. You will learn the five-phase transaction flow starting from a client application constructing a signed proposal, through endorsement and assembly, to ordering, validation, and final ledger commitment. We will also walk through the high-level setup steps for a multi-organization network: defining topology, generating cryptographic identities, producing configuration artifacts, deploying components, creating channels, and activating chaincode. A concrete example you will keep in mind is a two-organization test network where a client asks both organizations to endorse an asset transfer; we will use that to explain endorsement policies and version concurrency checks. As you follow the sequence, pay attention to common points of failure: missing certificates, mis-set environment variables, or incorrect endorsement policy definitions can stop a transaction or a channel from forming. By the end of this chapter you should be able to trace where to look when a transaction is rejected and what artifacts are required to bring up a minimal Fabric network. Reflect on which step — identity, endorsement, ordering, or validation — most affects security in your environment.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to trace a full transaction lifecycle and identify where each component participates. First, you will map the journey from a client-constructed, signed transaction proposal through endorsement, assembly, ordering, and final validation and commitment on the ledger. Second, you will explain how endorsing peers produce read/write sets and signed proposal responses and why peers do not update their ledger during endorsement. Third, you will outline the high-level steps required to create a multi-organization Fabric network: define topology, generate cryptographic material, produce configuration artifacts with configtxgen, deploy components, create channels, and deploy chaincode. Finally, you will recognize common points of failure—incorrect file paths, misconfigured environment variables, or broken endorsement policies—and apply basic debugging steps. These objectives guide what to practice: tracing a transaction, inspecting proposal responses, and running the cryptogen and configtxgen commands conceptually. Each skill matters because they let you design secure policies, locate failures fast, and set up a network that processes transactions predictably.

These objectives translate into practical abilities. You will be able to inspect a proposal response to verify endorsements and read/write sets, and then use that information to assemble and submit a transaction to the ordering service. You will understand why the ordering service only sequences transactions and does not execute chaincode, which helps you reason about where performance bottlenecks occur. On the setup side, you will conceptually run cryptogen to create MSP directories and then use configtxgen to generate a genesis block and channel transactions that embed those MSPs. A common example is generating crypto material for two organizations, then producing a channel transaction that lists them both so they can participate. Finally, you will practice troubleshooting steps: checking file paths, verifying that the MSP directories exist, confirming that environment variables like the Fabric config path are set correctly, and examining endorsement policy definitions in the channel config. These practical checks help you move from understanding to applying and maintaining a Fabric network.

Let's walk through the canonical five-phase transaction flow as a single, connected process. First, a client application constructs a transaction proposal. This proposal names a chaincode function, passes arguments, specifies a channel, and is signed with the client's X.509 identity. For example, a Node. js client might prepare a transfer from account A to account B and sign the proposal with its certificate. Second, the proposal goes to endorsing peers. Each endorsing peer verifies the client's signature, executes the chaincode against its local state database, and produces a read/write set and a signed proposal response. Remember: peers do not write state at this phase. Third, the client collects endorsements as required by the endorsement policy, assembles them with the original proposal and its signature, and submits the assembled transaction to the ordering service. An everyday misconception is to expect the ordering service to validate endorsements; it does not. Fourth, the ordering service sequences transactions into blocks, signs them, and broadcasts blocks to committing peers. Fifth, each committing peer validates endorsements against policy and performs a version concurrency control check to ensure read-set versions are still current. If both checks pass, the write set is applied and the block appended; if not, the transaction is recorded as invalid but stays on the chain. Think of execution and endorsement as a hypothesis check and ordering as the shared timeline that gives all peers the same view of history.

A transaction proposal is the client's initial request to execute a chaincode function. It contains the chaincode name, the function to invoke, any arguments, the channel identifier, and it is cryptographically signed by the client's identity. For example, a client asking chaincode to create an asset will include the asset fields as arguments and sign the proposal with its X.509 certificate and private key. When an endorsing peer receives the proposal, it verifies the client's signature to authenticate the request and then simulates execution of the chaincode against its local state. The important result here is the read/write set: the peer records which ledger keys were read and which keys would be written. The peer packages the read/write set into a proposal response and signs that response with the peer's private key to create an endorsement. A recurring misconception is to think a peer commits state at endorsement time; it does not. The endorsement is simply a cryptographic attestation that the peer, given its current state, produced that read/write set. Understanding this separation helps you reason about why read versions matter for later VCC checks and why collecting the correct set of endorsements is critical to satisfy policy before submission.

After you receive proposal responses, the client must collect the endorsements required by the chaincode's endorsement policy and assemble them into a single transaction. Assembly means bundling the original proposal, every collected endorsement, and the client's own signature into a transaction envelope. For example, if the endorsement policy requires signatures from Org1 and Org2, you need at least one signed response from a peer in each organization. Only a fully assembled, signed transaction can be submitted to the ordering service. A common misunderstanding is to assume the client should wait for ordering to validate endorsements; ordering only sequences transactions and does not evaluate endorsement policies. When the assembled transaction is sent to the ordering service, it becomes part of the global input stream the orderer uses to produce blocks. If endorsements are insufficient or missing, committing peers will later mark the transaction invalid during validation. So as a developer or operator, you must ensure the client is programmed to gather the required endorsements and to handle the case where endorsements fail or peers return different read/write sets. The client should also sign the assembled transaction to prove origin during ordering and later validation.

The ordering service's purpose is to create a single deterministic sequence of transactions for all peers. It receives fully assembled transactions from clients across organizations, arranges them chronologically according to its consensus algorithm, groups them into blocks, and then signs and broadcasts those blocks to all committing peers on the channel. For example, transactions from different clients are interleaved into an ordered stream so every peer processes the same sequence when validating and committing. The ordering service does not execute chaincode or validate endorsement policies — its responsibility is sequencing and availability. A practical implication is that ordering performance influences throughput and latency: batch timeouts and batch sizes affect how quickly a transaction appears in a block. A typical misconception is expecting the orderer to resolve endorsement conflicts. It cannot; if two transactions conflict on the same state, the first that commits will make the second fail its VCC check at commit time. Understanding this separation helps operators tune batch parameters and architects decide where to place ordering nodes and how many are needed for fault tolerance. Ordering Service Role and Block Formation means order only sequences and groups transactions into blocks; peers are responsible for validation and state changes.. In practical terms, sequencing, batching, and block distribution. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

When a committing peer receives a block, it processes each transaction in order and performs two key checks before applying any write set. The first is endorsement policy validation: the peer verifies that the collected endorsements satisfy the chaincode's policy, confirming the right organizations signed the proposal response. The second is the version concurrency control check, which ensures that the ledger state read by the endorsing peers has not changed since endorsement. This is implemented by comparing the read set versions recorded at endorsement time with the current versions in the state database. If both checks pass, the peer applies the write set and appends the block; if either fails, the transaction is marked invalid and its write set is not applied. An important consequence is that transactions are still visible on the blockchain when invalid; the record exists but has no effect on state. A common mistake is to confuse an invalid transaction with a missing record. Even failed transactions are recorded, which preserves an auditable trail. This mechanism ensures consistency across peers and prevents stale endorsements from changing up-to-date state.

Before you generate crypto or configuration artifacts you must decide on network topology: how many organizations will participate, how many peers each organization runs, and how many orderer nodes are required for the chosen consensus. For a minimal two-organization development network you might select one peer per organization and a single ordering node; for production you would plan multiple peers and a fault-tolerant orderer cluster. These choices affect endorsement policies, availability, and fault tolerance. For example, an endorsement policy requiring endorsements from three organizations implies you must have at least that many participating signing identities. A common mistake is configuring an endorsement policy that references organizations or MSP IDs that are not included in the channel configuration; this prevents transactions from ever meeting policy. Another frequent issue is under-sizing the ordering service which causes high latency under load. The topology decision also informs your cryptographic material generation: each organization needs its own MSP and CA roots embedded in genesis and channel artifacts. Treat topology as an architectural decision that sets constraints for every following setup step. Generating cryptographic material creates the identities and trust anchors that every component uses. In development you can use the cryptogen utility to produce X.509 certificates and private keys for orderers, peers, and users. For example, a typical command is: cryptogen generate --config=./crypto-config. yaml --output=./organizations. The crypto-config file lists organizations, domains, and node counts. After running cryptogen you should see MSP directories for each org under the output path, containing certificates and keystore material. A helpful self-check is to inspect organizations/peerOrganizations/org1. example. com/msp to confirm the admincerts and cacerts entries exist. Remember that production environments typically use Fabric CA instead of cryptogen to support dynamic enrollment and certificate lifecycle management. A common setup mistake is pointing configtxgen or peer commands at the wrong FABRIC_CFG_PATH; if the environment variable is unset or points to a different folder, commands will fail or produce artifacts referencing incorrect paths. Conceptually, cryptogen results become the identities that configtxgen will embed into genesis and channel artifacts. After you have MSPs and identity material, you use configtxgen to create the ordering system's genesis block and the channel configuration transactions. configtxgen reads configtx. yaml which declares Profiles, Organizations, and capabilities. For example: configtxgen -profile TwoOrgsOrdererGenesis -outputBlock./system-genesis-block/genesis. block creates the genesis block for the ordering service. Then use configtxgen -profile TwoOrgsChannel -outputCreateChannelTx./channel-artifacts/channel. tx -channelID mychannel to create the channel creation transaction. These artifacts embed MSP identifiers so ordering and channels recognize which organizations participate. An important step is generating anchor peer update transactions for each org, which tell the channel how peers are discovered. A common file-related mistake is failing to set FABRIC_CFG_PATH to the directory containing configtx. yaml; configtxgen will not find profiles or MSP directories and will produce incorrect or missing outputs. Conceptually, configtxgen ties the identities produced by cryptogen into the network's structural policies and initial state, making it an essential bridge between cryptographic identity and operational configuration. With artifacts generated you deploy the runtime components and bring them into channels. For development this often means Docker Compose to run Fabric CA servers, orderer nodes, and peer containers. For production you will use orchestration platforms such as Kubernetes. Once peers and orderers are running, create the channel using the channel transaction and have peers join the channel with peer channel join. Next, deploy chaincode using the lifecycle approach: package the chaincode, install it on peers, approve the definition from each organization, and then commit the chaincode definition to the channel. A concrete example sequence is: create channel, have peer0. org1 and peer0. org2 join, then package and install the chaincode on both peers, approve the chaincode for each org, and commit the chaincode definition. When bringing up a Fabric network or troubleshooting a failed transaction there are recurring root causes to check first. One common class of failures is file and path misconfiguration: cryptographic materials or MSP directories referenced by peers or configtxgen are missing or pointed at the wrong location. Inspecting the expected MSP paths under your organizations output folder often reveals the issue. Another frequent problem is environment variables like FABRIC_CFG_PATH not pointing to the directory containing configtx. yaml and connection profiles; this causes config commands to produce incorrect artifacts. Network connectivity or firewall rules can prevent peers and orderers from communicating, so verify that the advertised hostnames and ports are reachable. Mis-specified endorsement policies in the channel configuration are a logical error: if the policy requires endorsements from organizations not present on the channel, transactions will never meet policy. Performance bottlenecks often stem from small peer resources or orderer batch settings that create latency under load. A simple debugging workflow: confirm MSPs exist, verify environment variables, check logs for signature verification failures, and ensure endorsement policy matches intended organizations. This focused checklist helps you quickly find the likely cause before deeper investigation.

Security and maintainability are essential for a healthy Fabric network. At a minimum, protect private keys and MSP directories generated by cryptogen or Fabric CA: these artifacts are the root of trust for organizations, peers, and orderers. Use strong, unique passwords for CA servers and limit access to folders containing keystores. Back up critical configuration files and ledger data regularly so you can recover from node failure or data loss. Another practical point is to rotate certificates and plan for revocation in production environments, which is why Fabric CA is recommended for lifecycle management in non-development contexts. When debugging, never expose private keys or paste them into logs; treat keys as highly sensitive secrets. A frequent misconception is believing development shortcuts like sharing admin keys are harmless; they are acceptable only in isolated test networks and become severe risks in production. Finally, create operational runbooks that document the steps to recreate or restore MSP and config artifacts so teams can recover quickly. These maintenance habits reduce downtime and prevent accidental security breaches. Let's consolidate the essential concepts you saw in this chapter. First, the transaction flow is a sequence of phases: proposal, endorsement, assembly, ordering, and validation/commitment. Each phase has a distinct responsibility. Second, a transaction proposal originates from the client and contains the invocation details and client signature; it is not the committed transaction. Third, an endorsement is a peer's cryptographic signature over a proposal response that contains the read/write set resulting from executing chaincode against the peer's local state. These three concepts form the backbone of how Fabric ensures that only properly authorized, non-conflicting transactions change ledger state. Keep these definitions in mind as you trace transactions or generate configuration artifacts, because they point to where you should inspect signatures, versions, and policies when debugging.
